newsitem.title: GERMANY: Berlin gives Bosnian refugees marching orders.
newsitem.headline: Berlin gives Bosnian refugees marching orders.

text.p: Berlin authorities said on Tuesday they had started telling Bosnian refugees they were no longer welcome in Germany and that they had four weeks to leave the country.

A spokeswoman for Berlin's interior ministry said that 1,500 unmarried people and childless couples as well as 350 refugees who had arrived after the Dayton peace accord was signed in December had to leave by the end of October.

"Berlin has also been destroyed," said spokeswoman Francine Jobatey, referring to the city's World War Two devastation, "And the older generation has been particularly supportive of our decision to help these people but also to send them back."
"They know it is not easy to rebuild a country, but somebody has got to do it," she said. Those traumatised by the war could stay until the end of their therapy, she said.
German states last month ignored international criticism and decided to begin the gradual repatriation of some 320,000 war refugees starting from October 1.

Several states such as Berlin, Bremen, Baden-Wuerttemberg, Saxony and Bavaria said they would begin the repatriation programme immediately and expected the first departures this month and after that -- the first deportations.
But others such as North Rhine-Westphalia and Lower Saxony, heeding refugee agencies' advice, said they would wait until the spring and warmer weather before forcing anyone to go.

Bosnian refugees, who turned up to renew their residence permits at an office in Berlin's Hohenschoenhausen district, left in despair after being told they had to go. Many said it was impossible to return to their homes which had been destroyed and were in areas controlled by other ethnic groups.
"Winter is very harsh there. You can't send people back in the winter. We don't have the strength to solve these problems alone," said Moslem Nesad Dajic.

"If they send us back now we will die," said Dajic, 40, who fled advancing Bosnian Serb forces that took his home town, Modrica in northern Bosnia four years ago and found refuge in Berlin with his extended family.
Germany has taken in more Bosnian refugees than the rest of the European Union combined. The 320,000 here amount to nearly 10 percent of Bosnia's population.
Haunted by their own memories of war and its aftermath, many Germans at first took in the Bosnians with open arms.

While there is still widespread sympathy for the Bosnians, the country's more financially strapped states say they simply cannot afford the millions of marks it costs to house and feed the refugees indefinitely.

The federal government in Bonn and the regional states launched a campaign earlier this year to encourage refugees to go home. The government has offered to pay for their transport back and set up an employment agency to find them jobs there.
"Yes, we must rebuild Bosnia, but we need money for this. Without money, without building materials, without a place to build it's not possible," Dajic said.

"This deportation is like the genocide against the Bosnians (Moslems)," said Seherzada Malkic, 25, Dajic's sister-in-law, who emerged from the office crying after she had also been told she would be an illegal alien after four weeks.
Malkic said it would be impossible for her and her family to return to Modrica at present because it was controlled by Bosnian Serbs, who she said had originally chased them out.
When asked how she felt about going home, she said: "I can't trust these people (Serbs) anymore. I could never live alongside them ever again."
